topic_summary: Analysis of the Renaissance humanist reconstruction of Classical Latin from medieval Latin practice. The central question is whether humanist Classical Latin represented continuous evolution from medieval usage or a radical reconstruction from textual sources—whether the reconstructed form was reachable from the drifted vernacular or required symbolic reoccupation of an abandoned kernel.

key_entities: Petrarch (1304-1374, initiator of textual recovery vocation)
Vulgate (Latin Bible translation, source of medieval peculiarities)
key_tensions: Living drift vs textual reconstruction (medieval users vs humanist philologists)
Vernacular phonology vs reconstructed classical pronunciation (local sound systems vs Erasmian reform)
Organic vocabulary expansion vs classical purism (medieval technical terms vs Ciceronian lexicon)
Continuity vs rupture (evolutionary change vs symbolic reoccupation)
key_mechanisms: Ad fontes recovery (manuscript hunting, transcription, circulation of classical texts)
Grammatical codification (Valla's Elegantiae, Tortelli's De orthographia establishing classical norms)
Orthographic purification (insistence on ae/oe diphthongs, t/c distinction vs medieval simplifications)
key_absences: Absence of living native speakers to adjudicate correctness (no community of practice, only textual authority)
Absence of institutional enforcement mechanism for humanist reforms in vernacular-adjacent domains (law, medicine, science)

commitment_system_recognition.kernel_description: The Latin language as authoritative medium for learned discourse, grounded in textual exemplars from Roman antiquity
commitment_system_recognition.authority_description: Textual fidelity to classical authors (Cicero, Virgil) as interpreted by humanist philologists; no living native speakers to adjudicate

readings.commitment: Medieval Latin is the legitimate continuation of classical Latin through organic linguistic change
readings.authority_grounding: Living practice of educated users; functional adequacy for contemporary domains (theology, law, science)
readings.expected_structural_delta: Low extractiveness; vernacular phonology and expanded vocabulary treated as natural evolution; no victim set (medieval users are legitimate inheritors)

readings.commitment: Classical Latin is a fixed textual standard requiring reconstruction from ancient sources; medieval usage is corruption
readings.authority_grounding: Textual fidelity to Cicero/Virgil as interpreted by humanist philologists; ad fontes recovery as moral-intellectual vocation
readings.expected_structural_delta: High extractiveness; medieval practice delegitimized; victim set includes medieval scholars, vernacular-adjacent technical domains where classical purity is unattainable

readings.commitment: Classical norms apply to literary/rhetorical domains; medieval forms remain legitimate for technical/practical domains
readings.expected_structural_delta: Moderate extractiveness; bifurcated legitimacy creates status hierarchy (literary > technical); partial victim set (technical writers pressured toward unattainable classical standards)

axiom_contradictions.basis: Continuity reading treats linguistic change as legitimate evolution; rupture reading treats post-classical change as corruption requiring reversal. No single framework can hold both 'organic change is legitimate' and 'organic change is corruption' simultaneously.

omegas.description: Was classical Latin reachable from medieval Latin through continuous reform, or did it require symbolic reoccupation of an abandoned kernel? The rupture reading treats it as unreachable (requiring textual reconstruction); the continuity reading treats medieval forms as legitimate evolution. The hybrid reading suggests partial reachability (literary domains yes, technical domains no).
omegas.source: Core kernel contest; user's D1 break flag

omegas.description: Was Erasmian pronunciation a genuine reconstruction of ancient Roman speech or a scholarly construct? No living speakers exist to adjudicate; textual evidence (spelling, meter, grammarian descriptions) is incomplete. Pronunciation is the only domain where 'Ecclesiastical' and 'Classical' Latin can be presented as competing standards rather than literary subsets.
omegas.source: Deferred axis pronunciation_authority_vacuum; absence of native speaker community

omegas.description: If humanists had not imposed classical standards, would Latin have evolved into a pan-European learned vernacular (like medieval Latin was becoming) rather than fragmenting into national vernaculars? The rupture reading's high extractiveness may have accelerated Latin's abandonment for technical domains.
omegas.source: Deferred axis domain_bifurcation; Dark Matter Probe 3 (beneficiary scan)

omegas.description: What grounds the authority of textual exemplars (Cicero, Virgil) over living practice? The rupture reading assumes textual fidelity is self-evidently superior to functional adequacy. This assumption is contested by the continuity reading but not examined within either framework.
omegas.source: Dark Matter Probe 2 (absence inventory); unexamined premise of humanist philology

fracture_scan.notes: No fractures detected. Kernel/reading decomposition applied as specified. Three readings selected capture the structural topology: continuity (low ε, medieval practice legitimate), rupture (high ε, classical reconstruction delegitimizes medieval), hybrid (moderate ε, domain-specific bifurcation). Axiom contradiction declared between continuity and rupture readings (organic change as legitimate vs organic change as corruption). Deferred axes document structural preconditions and downstream consequences without adding independent constraint dimensions.
